entries.clue: Topless stunts engrossing husband in dockers’ milieu (6)

annotation.definitionNote: The answer is plural while 'milieu' is singular; the wharfs together make up the dockers' world.

indicatorNotes.Topless: the top (first) letter of the word is removed
indicatorNotes.engrossing: to engross is to absorb, so the shortened word takes the H inside it

blocks.note: stunts = DWARFS (verb, stunts growth), minus its first letter D
h = husband, the standard abbreviation; goes inside after the W

annotation.surface: Scandalous topless stunts performed by a husband down at the docks.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Stunts' looks like a noun about daredevilry, but it is the verb: to stunt growth is to dwarf. Behead DWARFS and wrap it round H.
annotation.definitionFit: Wharfs are the quays where dockers load and unload ships, the setting of their working life.

entries.clue: Struggle, insanely bored: it’s what you have to wear (8)

annotation.definition: it’s what you have to wear

indicatorNotes.insanely: done madly, so the letters of 'bored' are scrambled

blocks.note: a war is a struggle
anagram of BORED

annotation.surface: Someone grumbling, bored out of their mind, about the clothes they are forced to wear.
annotation.walkthrough: The definition is a whole phrase: a wardrobe can mean the stock of clothes a person owns, the things they have to wear.
annotation.definitionFit: Your wardrobe is your collection of clothes, everything you have available to put on.

entries.clue: Bow stored in cedar chest (3)

indicatorNotes.stored in: the answer is kept inside the following words

blocks.note: cedAR Chest

annotation.surface: An archer's bow put away in a cedar chest.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Bow' here is a curve, not the weapon the surface suggests.
annotation.definitionFit: A geometric sense: the curve of a bent archer's bow traces part of a circle, which is exactly what an arc is.

entries.clue: Model wearing elaborate headgear: wow! (5,4)

indicatorNotes.wearing: the model has the hat on, so the hat goes round it

blocks.note: fancy = elaborate, hat = headgear; split after FANCY to take T
the Model T Ford, so Model = T

annotation.surface: A fashion model on the catwalk in an extravagant hat, drawing gasps.
annotation.walkthrough: The model is not a person but the Model T, Ford's famous early car, which gives just the letter T.
annotation.definitionFit: 'Fancy that!' is an exclamation of surprise, just like 'wow!'.

entries.clue: It must be approximately a foot in length (4,4)

annotation.definition: It must be approximately a foot in length

blocks.note: the surface reading: about twelve inches long, a measurement
the meant reading: a human foot, whose shape and size the object copies

annotation.surface: A measuring puzzle: something that has to be about twelve inches long.
annotation.walkthrough: 'A foot' reads as the unit of twelve inches, but it is the body part: a shoe tree is shaped like a foot so it has to be roughly that long.
annotation.definitionFit: A shoe tree is a foot-shaped insert kept in a shoe to hold its shape, so it is sized like a foot.

entries.clue: He’d gab and grumble affectedly – tried to subtly impress (6-7)

indicatorNotes.affectedly: in an artificial, put-on manner, so the letters are rearranged

blocks.note: anagram fodder, 13 letters; 'and' just joins the pieces

annotation.surface: A man who chatters and moans in a put-on way, secretly fishing for admiration.
annotation.walkthrough: The fodder skips 'and': HE'D + GAB + GRUMBLE gives exactly the thirteen letters.
annotation.definitionFit: To humble-brag is to boast while pretending to be modest or complaining, a sly attempt to impress.

entries.clue: More paintings etc by O’Keeffe finally put up (5)

indicatorNotes.finally: take the last letter of O'Keeffe
indicatorNotes.put up: in a down clue, putting up reverses the letters

blocks.note: art = paintings and so on
by = X, as in 3 by 4 = 3 × 4
last letter of O'KeeffE

annotation.surface: More of Georgia O'Keeffe's paintings are being hung on the gallery wall.
annotation.walkthrough: Georgia O'Keeffe was an American painter, which makes 'by' look like authorship; here it is the multiplication sign X.
annotation.definitionFit: Extra means additional, more of something.

entries.clue: Sinking in Tigris, green, flailing (11)

indicatorNotes.flailing: thrashing about, so the letters are jumbled

blocks.note: anagram fodder, 11 letters

annotation.surface: An inexperienced swimmer flailing and going under in the River Tigris.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Sinking in' pictures drowning, but it means an idea being understood.
annotation.definitionFit: When a fact is registering, it is sinking in: being taken in and understood.

entries.clue: Go back, not initially finding exit (6)

indicatorNotes.not initially: 'initially' points at the first letter, and 'not' says that letter is missing

blocks.note: go back = REGRESS, minus its first letter R

annotation.surface: Someone retracing their steps, unable at first to find the way out.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface makes going back sound like the search for the exit, when it is the word that loses its R to become one.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym from Latin egressus, 'gone out': the word names the way out of a building or place.

entries.clue: Again give credence to description of Navy Seals outfit? (9)

blocks.note: to accept or back up something as true once more
the SEALs are a US special forces unit known for scouting work; 'outfit' here means a company or firm, and the '?' flags a jokey description

annotation.surface: Backing up a story about an elite US special forces unit.
annotation.walkthrough: The second half splits the answer as RECON FIRM: the Navy SEALs are a US special forces unit, and a firm doing recon (reconnaissance) is a fair, jokey description.
annotation.definitionFit: To reconfirm is to confirm again, to back up once more what you had given credence to.

entries.clue: Before perhaps, ladies in trouble (13)

indicatorNotes.Before: tells you where IN goes: in front of the ladies

blocks.note: used as itself, placed first
a ladies is one kind of public convenience, hence 'perhaps'

annotation.surface: Some women got into difficulties shortly before.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Ladies' means a women's public toilet; in Britain a public toilet is called a convenience, and the ladies is an example of one.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: being put to some trouble or bother is suffering an inconvenience.

entries.clue: Somewhat anti-German, this beast (5)

indicatorNotes.Somewhat: only part of the following words is used

blocks.note: anTI-GERman

annotation.surface: A creature with some hostility toward Germans.
annotation.walkthrough: The hyphen in anti-German hides the join between TI and GER.
annotation.definitionFit: Definition by example, with 'this' pointing at the hidden word: the striped big cat is one kind of wild beast.

entries.clue: Non-drinker wearing beam? No: irritable! (5)

indicatorNotes.wearing: the beam has the non-drinker on, so it goes round TT

blocks.note: a ray is a beam of light; split RA...Y
TT = teetotal, a non-drinker

annotation.surface: A teetotaller asked to wear a smile, snapping back that they're too grumpy.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Beam' looks like a smile to wear, but it is a ray of light, which holds TT.
annotation.definitionFit: Ratty is an informal British word for bad-tempered or irritable.

entries.clue: Like forward planning a mass exodus (11)

annotation.definition: Like forward planning a mass exodus

blocks.note: the surface reading: organising ahead of time; the meant reading: a stock phrase whose adjective adds nothing
a second stock phrase of the same kind, not the thing being planned

annotation.surface: Organising the logistics for a whole population to leave at once.
annotation.walkthrough: Read it as two examples, 'forward planning' and 'a mass exodus', rather than one plan: all planning is forward and every exodus is mass, so both say the same thing twice.
annotation.definitionFit: A tautologous phrase repeats its meaning needlessly, as both examples do.

entries.clue: Having chewed escallops, comes to premature end (9)

indicatorNotes.Having chewed: chewed food is broken up, so the letters are mixed

blocks.note: anagram fodder, 9 letters

annotation.surface: A diner eats some scallops and promptly keels over.
annotation.walkthrough: Escallops is an old spelling of scallops, which supplies exactly the letters needed.
annotation.definitionFit: A plan or venture that collapses fails and ends before its time.

entries.clue: Standard wedding feature in Britain: bold drunkard, first to trip (8,5)

indicatorNotes.first: the bold drunkard is placed at the front

blocks.note: b = bold, as in typefaces
a lush is a heavy drinker
used as itself
GB = Great Britain
a ride is a trip

annotation.surface: A British wedding where the obligatory drunken guest is the first to stumble.
annotation.walkthrough: 'In Britain' reads as scene-setting but is two separate chunks, and 'first' is a placement instruction for the bold drunkard, not a hint about an initial letter.
annotation.definitionFit: The blushing bride is the stock figure of every wedding, a standard feature of the day.

entries.clue: Seriously, I’m approaching Robin’s home (2,7)

blocks.note: I'm approaching = I am near: I + NEAR
a robin lives in a nest

annotation.surface: Someone solemnly announcing they are getting close to Robin's house.
annotation.walkthrough: Robin looks like a person's name, but it is the bird, whose home is a nest.
annotation.definitionFit: An idiom: meaning something 'in earnest' is meaning it sincerely, not as a joke, so it swaps for 'seriously'.

entries.clue: Goes to join with senior teachers’ backing (5,3)

blocks.note: heads = head teachers, who run schools
if you are for something, you back it

annotation.surface: Someone moving to a new school with the support of its head teachers.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Backing' looks like a reversal instruction, but it is simply FOR, meaning in support.
annotation.definitionFit: A phrasal verb: it describes the direction someone is travelling, so it swaps for 'goes to' in a sentence.

entries.clue: Avoiding adventurousness, having eaten dishes of bananas (2,3,4,4)

indicatorNotes.bananas: slang for crazy, so the letters go wild

blocks.note: anagram fodder, 13 letters

annotation.surface: A cautious diner who sticks to plates of bananas rather than risk anything exotic.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Bananas' looks like the food on the dishes, but it means mad and scrambles the words before it.
annotation.definitionFit: Staying on the safe side means taking no risks, avoiding anything adventurous.

entries.clue: In the wrong order, finally arrive in hilly area (6)

indicatorNotes.In the wrong order: the two words of 'land up' are swapped

blocks.note: the UP of 'land up', meaning to end up
to land is to arrive

annotation.surface: A traveller who took the roads in the wrong order and eventually reached the hills.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Finally arrive' is LAND UP; putting the phrase in the wrong order gives UP LAND.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: the word names the higher ground of a region, as opposed to lowland, and such country is hilly.

entries.clue: Looking up and swearing (9)

blocks.note: improving, as in 'things are looking up'
vowing or pledging, as in swearing an oath

annotation.surface: Someone gazing skyward while cursing.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Looking up' means improving, as in 'things are looking up', and 'swearing' is vowing, not cursing.
annotation.definitionFit: Promising means showing signs of improving, and also pledging or swearing to do something.

entries.clue: Conclude fashionable arbiter must be sent up (5)

indicatorNotes.must be sent up: in a down clue, sending up turns the arbiter upside down, reversing it

blocks.note: in = fashionable
a ref (referee) is an arbiter

annotation.surface: A verdict that a trendy referee deserves to be mocked.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Sent up' suggests mockery, but in a down clue it means read upwards.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: the word means reaching a conclusion by reasoning from evidence.

entries.clue: Stiff clothing Everyman had (5)

blocks.note: a rig or rig-out is an outfit of clothing
Everyman is the setter, so 'Everyman had' = I had = I'D

annotation.surface: The setter recalls wearing some stiff, uncomfortable clothes.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Clothing' wants to be a container indicator, but it is the noun RIG; the setter's name stands for I.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: something that will not bend or flex is both stiff and rigid.

entries.clue: Primarily antisocial, leerily offish or frosty? (5)

annotation.definition: Primarily antisocial, leerily offish or frosty?

indicatorNotes.Primarily: take the first letter of each following word

blocks.note: Antisocial Leerily Offish Or Frosty

annotation.surface: A list of cold, standoffish traits, asking which one fits.
annotation.walkthrough: The whole clue is both the definition and the wordplay: every word describes someone aloof, and their initials spell it.
annotation.definitionFit: An aloof person is cool and distant, antisocial and frosty.

entries.clue: Showed approval of France (wasn’t paying attention) (6,3)

blocks.note: nodding shows agreement
used as itself
F is the international vehicle code for France

annotation.surface: Someone gave France the nod without really listening.
annotation.walkthrough: The brackets make the definition look like an aside, when it is the definition itself.
annotation.definitionFit: Someone who nodded off fell asleep, so was not paying attention.

entries.clue: Possess fancy item of clothing that’s no good (3)

indicatorNotes.that’s no good: the G for good is taken away

blocks.clueFragment: fancy item of clothing that’s no good
blocks.note: a fancy item of clothing = GOWN, minus G (good)

annotation.surface: Owning a fancy outfit that turns out to be useless.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Fancy' here is part of describing a gown, not an anagram instruction; G = good is the standard abbreviation.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: having something as your property means you possess it.

entries.clue: Tactful and distinct in pronouncement (8)

indicatorNotes.in pronouncement: when spoken, the word sounds like the answer

blocks.note: discrete means distinct or separate, as in discrete units

annotation.surface: Praise for someone careful and clear in how they speak.
annotation.walkthrough: The two spellings are easily confused: discrete means separate, discreet means tactful.
annotation.definitionFit: A discreet person is tactful and careful not to embarrass others.

entries.clue: Pot-head, one preparing apricots? (6)

blocks.note: slang for a habitual cannabis smoker
a person taking the stones out of fruit

annotation.surface: A cannabis user in the kitchen getting fruit ready.
annotation.walkthrough: The second definition is playful: someone who removes the stones from apricots could be called a stoner.
annotation.definitionFit: A stoner is slang for a habitual cannabis user, a pot-head.
